en: The spiritual responses of the Śarīra manifest the principles of heaven and earth and the Way of the sages and worthies; among these, there are aspects that can be measured and those that cannot be measured.

That which can be measured is what the wise and the foolish alike have known throughout antiquity and the present. As for that which cannot be measured, even those who study to peer into the realm of the sages and whose talents penetrate [all fields of knowledge]...
Even the hundred schools of thought cannot clarify even a ten-thousandth part of this.
In the spring of the Wuxu year, I happened to pass by Fokuo Jingshe (Buddha-land Vihara) and visited Master Jisheng, where I met Master Shengbi.
Listening to his words, he was truly a noble gentleman of the Chan school. Master Ji and Master Sheng were fellow students; Master Ji propagated the Way in Bangjiang, while Master Sheng...
The Upādhyāya had retired to Mount Tiantai, where he drew blood to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Due to the height of his sincerity, a śarīra suddenly appeared at the tip of his brush.
The Upādhyāya was moved and informed me of it. At that time, I was suffering from a slight ailment;
when I treated it with consecrated water, the effect was extraordinary. I asked him, "Is what appeared at the tip of the brush truly a śarīra? [I addressed] the Upādhyāya by name.
He said, "That which appeared at the tip of my brush on that day was indeed a true śarīra.
Furthermore, it is not as if a śarīra cannot be seen today; it shall arrive in three days. I replied, "Yes, yes—and no, no.
After three days had passed, Master Sheng asked, "Did you see the śarīra yesterday? I replied, "The autumn air is high and clear, and colored clouds swirl about."
[He] circumambulated [it]. Regarding what was seen on this day, it could not yet be called a *śarīra*. The Upādhyāya said, "This is precisely what is called a *śarīra*.
Please explain its significance in detail. Now, *śarīra* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang, it means "body-bone.
Although nearly four thousand years have passed since the Tathāgata entered *parinirvāṇa*, his golden body can no longer be beheld, yet the *śarīra* remains perfectly intact.
As for those enshrined in golden stupas, they number eighty-four thousand; what is currently enshrined at Mount Yuyang in Siming is but one of these.
It was obtained when the monk Kang Senghui of Wu came from the Western Regions and sought śarīra, achieving success after twenty-one days.
To this day, it remains contained within the stupa and cannot be seen again. As for the various wonders of its manifested signs, they are beyond compare.
First: sometimes it rose as a crimson color, sometimes it emitted a turquoise light, sometimes it manifested as a string of pearls, and sometimes it revealed sacred images;
truly, these cannot be enumerated. As for the multicolored clouds witnessed yesterday—what else could they be but śarīras?

It is marvelous that what was once seen with the tip of a brush is now seen again within the autumnal sky. I said: "There are things that can be measured, and there are things that cannot be measured."
As for this, the nature of the śarīra is truly beyond my ability to fathom.
Whether what was previously seen at the tip of my brush was the śarīra, or whether what is now seen in the autumnal sky is the śarīra—
I have recorded these questions and answers in detail here, as requested by the Venerable Master.
Written with prostrations by Li Zhao of Laoshan on the third day before the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of Wuxu during the Kangxi era of the Great Qing.
Preface to the Circumstances of the Śarīra Repentance.
It is heard that in antiquity, those who were able to move heaven and earth and reach the spirits did so through nothing other than ultimate sincerity.
Thus, superior men of goodness experienced a necessary resonance with the divine; the numerous instances recorded in the annals are indeed beyond counting.
As for those whose virtue and character transcended the ordinary, their conduct stood far above the common flow and was not something that could be fathomed by those of shallow understanding.

How could it be within the reach of mere observation? That his divine responses were so manifest, yet remained rare to see and hear of in this world—regarding the Venerable Shengbi, I cannot help but have something to say.
I recall when I and the Master were both attending our late teacher at Mount Huqiu;
as for the conduct he had practiced in the past, his profound depth and expansive serenity already set him apart from the rest of the assembly.
How extraordinary! His bitter resolve to forget his own person for the sake of the Way was something that could not be matched by ordinary people.

Having retired to Mount Tiantai and shed his mortal shell from the world of men, he then cultivated all the secret Dharma-gates. Above, he offered libations to the vast compassion of the former sages;
below, he sought to awaken the ignorance of all living beings. Furthermore, with utmost sincerity, he pierced his own flesh with a needle and transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by hand.
As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and all other Mahāyāna sūtras, he recited them without ceasing, even amidst bitter cold or humid heat.

What manner of sincerity did he possess in his recitation, and what constancy did he maintain in guarding the Way? When he was transcribing the "Ten Faiths" chapter (*Daśa-śraddhā-varga*), his meditative wisdom became increasingly clear and his diligence redoubled;
thereupon, he was moved by the heavens to rain down fine rice, and lotus flowers grew from the earth. Furthermore, regarding his brush...

At the peak, he suddenly obtained śarīra relics. The marvel of this auspicious response was such that it surpassed anything found in the world; all who beheld it could not help but look up with admiration.
He sincerely propagated the news far and wide, regarding it as a supernatural wonder, and concluded that [the Master] must surely have been one who had attained the stage of fruition (*phala*).

From then on, the Master’s reputation grew even further; yet he remained humble and concealed his true nature. Taking the śarīra relics he had obtained, he visited famous mountains everywhere until the spring of the Wuxu year.
When he first visited me at Bon-hyang Bok-guk, he brought forth the śarīra he had obtained for me to behold.

I immediately entreated him to remain as a permanent resident and commissioned a bronze stūpa to enshrine them. The Master then sighed with deep emotion and said, "My original intention was to return to my place of training to offer them there;
however, my karmic conditions now lie here, and they cannot be shifted. Therefore, I shall sacrifice my own body and seek them once more."
Thereupon, he closed the gates to his north for a period of thirty days and nights, diligently and tirelessly prostrating before the Buddha.

He burned off an arm and recited the *Mahāratnakūṭa-vistara-cittānuparivartinī-dhāraṇī*, setting a specific date to seek its fulfillment. When the appointed time arrived, the response was indeed realized.

The fourfold assembly who came to witness this gathered like waters flowing to the sea; among all those who sought counsel from the Master, there were none who did not exclaim in wonder at the marvel. Thus it was.
The local gentry and officials of Yangzhou all turned to him with reverence. Alas! That which the Master performed may truly be called the revitalization of the Way for his time;
yet the Master further exercised his compassionate heart, [establishing that] wherever the śarīra were located...
He is no different from the Buddha. Having already obtained such an extraordinary opportunity, how could one fail to cultivate Buddhist practices to propagate them?
Thus, examining the past and investigating the present, he established this method of repentance, taking the śarīra as its core and divine mantras as its merit.
I desire that all the multitudes may practice with diligence, extinguish all transgressions, and fulfill all their aspirations. Alas!
We now live in the Dharma-ending age, and the Buddha-way has long been submerged. Were it not for relying on superior conditions, how could one be uplifted? Such was the Master.

This may be called parting the clouds of eternal night to bring forth the moon from the dark alleys of the world. Its compassionate light shines universally, leading the multitudes of sentient beings;

it spreads the wind of virtue far and wide, overflowing throughout the six directions. Those who come after and attain samādhi by relying on this method of repentance will naturally be able to carry on the tradition of the former sages and propagate the path of universal benefit.
How could its influence stop merely at moving heaven and earth and reaching the spirits and ghosts?
And that is all. Qianjiang Fuguo Yuandu bows and inscribes this regarding the nature of numinous awareness:
it enwraps the Great Void; the truth of wondrous enlightenment encompasses the sands of the world. When water freezes into ice—

Ordinary fools lose their penetrating illumination, like clouds parting to reveal the moon; the noble wisdom attains its lofty clarity, ensuring that the vast sky remains bright and mirror-like, never stirred by the clouds of ignorance.
One must look forward to the great ocean being windless and its waves of consciousness becoming calm and clear for the sake of these deluded masses.
Those who are entangled in the bonds of sweet affection and remain in a state of anxious agitation have not yet escaped the burdens of the physical form.

Therefore, the World-Honored One manifested in the Central Kingdom and strode beyond the three realms; looking down, he responded to the diverse capacities and desires of sentient beings, preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years to deliver all living beings.
In the night at the Śāla Grove, he entered parinirvāṇa. Out of compassion for this final age and desiring to benefit future generations, he shattered his vajra-body to form śarīras.
These were divided among eight kingdoms, each of which erected stūpas and temples; those two portions kept secret likewise possess their own sites of enlightenment.
Through his sincerity, the bronze ritual vessels emitted resonant sounds after twenty-one days; during Kang Seng’s observance of the six periods of fasting, the jade bowls radiated light.
Regarding these auspicious responses under Emperor Sui, they cannot be fully recounted. Having entered the Way in his childhood, he traveled to various regions after reaching adulthood.
Then, on the full moon of the second month in the spring of the year of Yiyou, he concealed his form at Mount Tai and hung his traveling hat upon Mount Huading, where he knelt long before the Buddha.
First, with a sincere heart, he made his vow. Incense smoke coalesced above his seat; the precious bowl reflected the light of the *candana* water. Flower buds held their fragrance;
the golden knife sliced through the "crescent-moon" blood [of the lotus]. He unrolled paper from the Shanyang Valley and ground ink at the Duan stone inkstone.

Red dots fell one by one like flying clouds adorning the wings of butterflies; thick green leaves hung down as the sound of gurgling springs harmonized with the howls of monkeys. Thus he transcribed the sutra.

While discussing the texts of the two assemblies and expounding upon the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), he frequently moved heaven to rain down corn and cause white flowers to spring up from the stone steps.
Auspicious signs of *śarīra* (relics) emerged from his pen, and bundles of *palm-leaf* manuscripts were arrayed upon his desk. Such things as these have never been seen in the degenerate age;

they constitute the eighty-one fascicles of the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya-sūtra*. After two full cycles of seasons had passed, he thereafter shifted his staff and traveled extensively throughout the six [directions].
In the moonlight he donned his fur robe; at dawn he chewed the snows of Mount Emei. With a staff leaning against a thousand crags, he stepped upon the ice of Mount Tai at dusk.
By the yam fires on the peaks of Heng, he shared the warmth with Lan Zan; within the meditative mind of Chicken Foot Mountain, the Dhūta monk alone smiled.

In the year Wuxu, when the sun was in the mansion of Daliang, he traveled to the Hall of the Head Preceptor at Fuguo Jingshe on Bang River, where, bound by the bond of fellow practitioners, he led the assembly.

He remained at the Salt Terrace (Yantai), where he realized his karmic ties from past lives. With utmost sincerity, he made offerings; thus, for forty-nine days, he established an altar and performed the Way.
On the morning of the full moon in the fifth month, the *śarīra* descended. Ten thousand people prostrated themselves, and thousands turned their hearts [to the Dharma].

They cast two pagodas to enshrine the golden remains and constructed a pavilion to pay homage. The jade casket was placed by the great river, where those on both banks alike looked up in reverence. Truly...

In this small courtyard of ritual observance, we dwell in profound seclusion as the Dharma community is once again opened. Auspicious clouds swirl above the pinnacle of the *stūpa*, and fragrant breezes waft through the bells of the *toraṇa*.
Your spiritual power is boundless and the wheel of your vows has already turned; your numinous penetration is manifest, and your wondrous responses are secretly directed.
Looking up, we repay the profound compassion of our Buddha who delivers us all, and we offer our highest prayers for [the Emperor].

May the imperial lineage enjoy long-lasting prosperity; may the merit accrue to the donors and its bounty extend throughout the great trichiliocosm. Now, as this text of repentance is being carved for printing, I have respectfully set forth the origins of its cause at the beginning.
I venture to inform my fellow practitioners that I shall cultivate reverence until the end of my life. Thus it is said.
The Table of Contents for the *Śarīra-kṣamaṇa-dharma* (Repentance Ritual for Relics) Autocomposed by Jiseng of Shenshi in Ancient Wu: 1.
Rigidly Purifying the Dharma Hall 2. Preparatory Expedient Means (*pūrvāṅga-upāya*)
Third, clearly explaining the intent of cultivation; fourth, burning incense and scattering flowers;
fifth, formally extending the ritual invitation; sixth, praising with a sincere heart;
seventh, offering devotion and bowing to the Buddha; eighth, fully performing repentance.
The Ninth: Reverently Chanting the Mantra-Heart; The Tenth: Making Vows and Dedication.
End of the Table of Contents for the *Śarīra Repentance Method*.
*Śarīra Repentance Method*.
Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Jiseng and edited by the Dingshan bhikṣu Yanzhang;
this repentance ritual is now being circulated, divided into ten sections for exposition.

First, one must establish the site of practice (maṇḍala) as a great place of the Way, prioritizing purity above all else. Only by doing so can the mind be gathered through the power of the environment, and the holy life (brahmacarya) be brought to fulfillment.
If one wishes to establish a platform for repentance, it should be done in a secluded and quiet location; a new hall or chamber should be constructed (a pre-existing room will not suffice).
[Remove] obstructions. Scrape away the old earth and, at a pure location, take fresh soil free of tiles and stones to fill the ground.
Anoint it with scented water until it is exceedingly pure and solemn. Above, suspend a white silk jeweled canopy proportionate to the size of the altar;
within the canopy, hang a mirror of the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan), and along the edges of the canopy, suspend five-colored tassels. Furthermore, within the canopy, hang five-colored jeweled banners.

Hang various silk streamers and multicolored banners throughout the hall; the flowers suspended there should vary in size so that they together resemble the manner in which devas and humans scatter blossoms.
In the center of the altar, offer to Śākyamuni Buddha, depicted in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
To his left, offer to Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, depicted in a wrathful form, holding a vajra in his right hand and a white fly-whisk in his left. To his right, offer to Maṇivajra Bodhisattva.

[Sa]. The left hand holds a precious jewel, and the right hand grasps a white whisk (it is not a hindrance if these do not correspond to the forms of the two Bodhisattvas; nevertheless, one should paint the forms according to the sūtras).
Before the image, arrange various fine flowers, as well as incense burners, altars, and other ornaments (these must be elegant, dignified, and in accordance with the Dharma).

At the center of the altar, offer a śarīra-relic stūpa (it is not a hindrance if there is none; it is appropriate to depict a painted stūpa). Surround the altar with mats (this is done out of concern for dampness on the ground).

The cushions shall be padded with soft cotton batting (using neither woolen rugs nor felt, as these are prohibited by the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*). Silk curtains shall be suspended all around the altar of purification, and no one at all shall be permitted to enter.
Those performing the ritual of repentance shall wear fresh, clean garments (if new clothes are unavailable, they may be washed and dyed; however, bathing is the primary requirement).

After bathing, they shall put them on before entering the ritual hall. Their shoes must be clean and orderly; they must not be disheveled (when entering the altar, they should be removed one by one in sequence).
Furthermore, the altar should be cleared out, as it must be replaced when it becomes worn. After bathing, one should put on clean robes; this should be done throughout the entire period.
Every day, one should prepare fresh, famous flowers, as well as various excellent vegetables and fresh fruits, to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
One must exert oneself to the utmost; only through such sincerity will there be a response. Twenty-four people shall descend into the altar space; more than this is not permitted.
Second, one should beforehand employ skillful means.
When a practitioner of ritual repentance is about to enter the dharma-hall, their body and mind may be distracted and disordered; they must therefore first employ skillful means.

One should prepare a separate room for seven days, not remaining day or night in the same place as the dharma-hall, to practice and familiarize oneself with the liturgical texts until they are thoroughly mastered.
The presiding repentant leader, together with their fellow practitioners, should maintain a level mind and tranquil breath to clarify the intent of the repentance and set forth its principles.
One should observe the etiquette for entering and leaving [the sanctuary], as well as the modulation of the Sanskrit chants (where harmony and gentleness are paramount).

One should also attend to dyeing, washing, mending, and sewing, as well as whatever duties are required during the period. All other worldly affairs and external distractions must be immediately set aside;

one should focus solely on sincerity, performing prostrations, repentance, and the recitation of mantras. By fulfilling these practices, one will surely attain the direct vision of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

O Great Bodhisattva, you shall certainly receive empowerment and the prediction of enlightenment. All that you seek shall be fulfilled according to your wishes; you shall obtain everything as you desire.

You must not for even a single thought-moment give rise to recollections of the five sensory objects (form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch). Diligently subdue the three poisons (greed, anger, and delusion) and forever sever craving and desire.
Since each person possesses, from time immemorial, the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization, you must perform the ritual methods to abandon them; only then will you not need to repent.

Regarding internal obstacles: the practitioner should contemplate which precepts have been violated and seek repentance with urgency and earnestness. If certain habits are particularly heavy, one should rebuke them and bring them into balance.
If one can ensure that the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are pure, then the path of resonance will be met, and one will spontaneously attain fulfillment according to one's wishes.
Third, to correctly clarify the intent of cultivation, one should examine that each of the various repentance rites has its own origin and its own primary tenet.

The Great Compassion Repentance was composed based on the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*, for the purpose of extinguishing all transgressions and perfecting the unsurpassed path. The Pure Land Repentance is based on the *Mahā-amitābha*... [text truncated]
The *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Contemplation of the Buddha of Infinite Life), the *Dundubhisvara-rāja Sūtra*, and the *Buddhabhāṣita Amitābha Sūtra*.
The *Practices and Vows of Repentance* was composed based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for the purpose of fulfilling the ten great kings of vows and directly transcending to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The *Bhaiṣajyaguru Repentance* was composed based on... [text continues]... for the purpose of eliminating all obstacles and seeking rebirth in Sukhāvatī so as to attain the stage of non-retrogression.

The *Bhaisajyaguru Sūtra Repentance* was composed for the purpose of eliminating calamities and misfortunes, prolonging life and extending one’s years, and swiftly ascending to the rank of Buddhahood.
The *Repentance of King Liang* was commissioned by imperial decree to rescue the suffering of the Xi clan;

it was compiled by various Dharma masters who gathered materials from the various Mahāyāna sūtras, intended to enable all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness. The *Water Repentance of Compassion* likewise originated from [the teachings of] Kāśyapa...

Venerable Nāgārjuna, using the water of samādhi, washed away karmic enmity; he composed this work extensively based on various Mahāyāna sūtras, desiring to explain all transgressions so that one may realize bodhi.

Other rites, such as the Śūraṅgama Repentance, the Gratitude Repentance, and the Kṣitigarbha Repentance, each have their own specific source of authority. This present Śarīra Repentance Method is likewise based upon these śarīras.
I have composed this with reverence, relying upon the *Mahāratnakūṭa-vistara-kūṭāgāra-susthita-rahasya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
desiring to eliminate all heavy obstructions, swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi, and personally behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because it fulfills all that is sought, the Sūtra says: "If a person merely hears the name of this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Established Secret Dhāraṇī, all evil destinies are extinguished.
Merely by recollecting this dhāraṇī, one has already made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to all the Buddhas of the ten directions. If...
Upon merely reciting it, one immediately attains non-retrogression toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Even after a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand kalpas, all the Tathāgatas would be unable to fully extol its merits, for their capacities would be exhausted.
This dhāraṇī possesses great majestic power; no māras whatsoever can ever create obstacles for it, nor can any enemies, wicked associates, ghosts, or spirits.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, non-humans, and others shall find no opportunity to harm them, and their immeasurable roots of goodness will increase.
If one merely recollects this dhāraṇī, they will obtain immeasurable merit; how much more so for those who can long recite and maintain it—their merit would be beyond calculation.
Even for those who complete ten thousand recitations, all things they seek shall be accomplished.
Therefore, I have carefully relied upon this original sutra to establish this method of repentance.

It is intended for practitioners of the Way so that by performing even a small amount of wholesome roots, they may obtain great benefit and merit, behold the Buddha in person, and receive empowerment. Compared to other methods of repentance, this is truly swift and essential.
What is most esteemed is the precision and single-mindedness of one’s practice; through such resonance with the divine, one will surely obtain their wishes.

To carefully determine the duration of the repentance period: according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is seven times seven days; according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it is three times seven days.

Furthermore, according to the *Dundubhisvara-rāja Sūtra* and the *Great Amitābha Sūtra*, it is ten days and ten nights; according to the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, it is seven days and seven nights. Based on these four [scriptures]...

Setting such a period—whether it be five days, three days, or even shorter (all of which are likewise expedient means)—the practitioner should focus the mind with single-minded intent for the full seven weeks, or down to three weeks, or even one week of day and night.
During these six periods [of the day], they should reverently worship the Buddha and recite the *dhāraṇī*, whether sitting or walking, never allowing the mind to become distracted.
They must not engage with outsiders, nor speak, converse, jest, or indulge in negligence and sleep. Relying on...

If the ritual is delayed, one should look up and down and blink; then, binding the breath and fixing the mind on the mantra, the heart shall seek a spiritual response. With single-minded diligence... [Question:
Since the ritual methods are so numerous, how can one maintain single-mindedness? [Answer: There are both principles and practices. Once one has entered the *maṇḍala*,...

With body and mind withdrawn and collected, like the moon in the vast sky, one responds to conditions according to circumstances while the fundamental essence remains unmoving; this is called "principle" (*li*).

When practicing single-mindedness, such as at the time of prostrating to the Buddha, one does not think of other dharmas. However, when exclusively prostrating to the Buddha or reciting mantras, if the mind recalls other texts:

Simply focus exclusively on reciting the mantra. As for all other dharmas, they are likewise merely names and matters. By attaining single-mindedness through this alone, one will surely fulfill one's wishes.
When approaching the period of repentance, purify yourself strictly overnight; take pure water and recite the Great Compassion Mantra twenty-one times over it.
Sprinkle [incense] in the various directions to establish the boundary.

Fourth, burn incense and scatter flowers (having thus purified the three karmas, enter the maṇḍala; having finished offering the incense, stand upright and contemplate as follows: "For the sake of sentient beings, I have resolved upon bodhicitta; because there is that which I seek and aspire for, I must generally discuss the Three Jewels and extensively cultivate offerings").
The Three Jewels, may you bestow your compassion and surely take heed of me. In accordance with my requests, please bear witness to my vows. First, one should chant:
"With all reverence and single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the eternally abiding Buddhas of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm."

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the eternally abiding Dharma throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm; with single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the eternally abiding Sangha throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm.
(Having completed the prostrations, the leader burns incense, scatters flowers, and says:)
All these members of the assembly each kneel with one knee raised, solemnly holding incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma (the assembly recites together):
"To the Triple Gem of the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm" (each person holding a hand-incense burner, they extensively perform the offering and chant).
Dwelling throughout the ten directions, may all Buddhas accept me.

To those who pervade the ten directions—those of the past and present, and all the World-Honored Ones of the future, as well as the Bodhisattvas of majestic virtue—I now pay homage to them all. (While reciting, visualize bowing down.)

(These fragrant flowers of mine pervade the ten directions, serving as subtle and wondrous luminous platforms. Therein are celestial music, divine precious incense, celestial delicacies, celestial precious robes, and inconceivable wondrous dharma-dusts. From each single dust mote emerge all dust motes; from each single dust mote emerge all buddha-lands.

They revolve without obstruction, mutually adorning one another, reaching everywhere before the Triple Gem in the ten directions and throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions. In every instance, my own body is present, performing offerings. Each and every offering pervades the entire dharma-realm; they are distinct yet without confusion or obstruction.

Until the end of the future, they perform the work of Buddhas, universally perfuming all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm. Upon being perfumed, they all give rise to the bodhicitta and together enter the state of non-arising, realizing the wisdom of the Buddha.)
Having stood up and made offerings,
one bows with full reverence (one prostration).
Fifth, one formally extends the invitation with a bow.

(Up to this point, the visualization and offerings have been completed. Now, add incense once more. Kneeling upright and holding the incense burner, arouse a heart of profound reverence and specifically entreat the Triple Gem to descend upon this ritual site; do not treat this lightly. To invite the Most Honored Ones, you must purify your three karmas and offer this invitation with single-minded devotion.

If you do not do so, the mere formality will be of no benefit. You should visualize all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, each according to their respective direction, leading their retinues and entering my ritual site as if they were present before your eyes.
Do not allow even a moment’s distraction, such as the snapping of fingers, from the time of the initial invitation. After the initial invitation, do not chant [the invocation] at other times).
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, our Original Teacher who now sits at the site of enlightenment:

(Śākyamuni is our teacher; he preached the Mahāyāna sūtras and enabled us to cultivate these wholesome dharmas. We should direct our minds to feel gratitude for this profound kindness. Hereafter, follow this pattern for three entreaties. At each entreaty, hold the incense burner, prostrate, and contemplate, saying:

"The true nature of the three karmas is like empty space; the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is likewise so. Without departing from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for the sake of sentient beings, he comes together with the assembly to receive our offerings.")

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the World-Honored One, King of Blazing Radiance Who Eliminates Calamities and Extends Life, from the Pūrṇacandra World in the East (the verse is identical, with the name changed as before; hereafter the same applies).
With single-minded devotion, I invoke the World-Honored One, Amitāyus, the Teacher of the West and Guide Who Leads the Way.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Ratnasambhava of the south;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Sūkṣma-jaya of the north;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Lokendra-sudarśana-mahā-vīrya.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Vicitramaṇiviśuddhapratiṣṭhita;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Sarvarūpasaṃdarśanaprabha;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara.
With single-minded devotion, we entreat the World-Honored One of Auspicious Marks and Radiance; with single-minded devotion, we entreat the World-Honored One of Sublime Sound;
with single-minded devotion, we entreat the World-Honored One of Immeasurable Voice;
with single-minded devotion, we entreat the World-Honored One of Great Pervasive Wisdom-Victory.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One, King of Liberation; with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One, King of Beautiful Sound.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One, Pure One; with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One, Pure Giver.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One, Sovereign King of Majestic Power; I entreat the World-Honored One, Immutable.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Maitreya; with single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Śarīraprabhāsarāja;

with single-minded devotion, I entreat all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, as far as the limits of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, as far as the limits of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

With single-minded devotion, I entreat all the precious stupas containing the relics of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as far as the limits of empty space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra-rāja and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Māyā, the Mother of Great Compassion.
With single-minded devotion, we entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Ākāśagarbha and Vajragarbha;
with single-minded devotion, we entreat the Bodhisattva Anantamati and the Night Goddess Prabhūtā.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the King of Secrets, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Subhūti;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhamati;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Samantacakṣus and Suhasaṃgama;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattvas Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Pūrṇagarbha;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who are the patriarchs of successive generations.

With single-minded devotion, we invite all the great Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Saṅgha of the ten directions and three periods of time throughout the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm. (The assembly chants:
With single-minded devotion, we invite Great Brahmā Deva-rāja, Śakra Devendra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, and those of the Desire, Form, and Formless Realms.
The Great Heavenly Kings, the various benevolent spirit-kings who obtain and protect the Buddha’s śarīra, stūpas, and monasteries while upholding dhāraṇīs,
the oceanic dragons, the eight classes of beings, and all deities of the celestial courts, the underworld, and those who traverse water, land, and air, together with their entire retinues.
I have invited the World-Honored Buddha Śākyamuni, the World-Honored Medicine Master Buddha of the eastern world,
Amitābha Buddha of the western world, as well as all the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions;
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and all the great [Bodhisattvas] of the ten directions.
O Bodhisattva, all you holy sages, we pray that you will not forsake your compassion and accept this humble sincerity.

With your omniscient wisdom and far-reaching vision of the Path, remaining inseparable from the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), please descend to this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), take your seat upon the Dharma-throne, and gather us in.
(One prostration) May you bear witness to these wholesome dharmas. As my practices and vows reach fulfillment, may all devas, māras, brahmās, Dharma-protecting benevolent deities,

nāgas, ghosts, and other assemblies, as well as all sages and worthies, respond to my invitation and arrive to oversee and guard this site of practice, protecting its purity so that we may together accomplish these wholesome deeds.

(Stand up and adjust your robes. After reciting the Three Refuges three times, call out, "Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. Exit the altar and enter the meditation hall. Once the incense offering is complete, attend to your own needs.)
(Below this, the actual ritual of repentance is clearly explained; at all other times, one proceeds from this point).
Sixth, wholeheartedly offer praise (ring the bell within the hall, assemble in unison, maintain a focused mind, direct one’s contemplation with devotion, and recite aloud).
Homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha (recite while entering the altar and taking one’s place).

With all reverence and single-minded devotion, we prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. (After the first prostration, the incense is burned, flowers are scattered, and the presiding officer announces:)

All these assemblies shall each kneel upon their right knees, reverently holding incense and flowers to make offerings to the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm (each holding a hand-incense burner and extensively performing the offering while chanting):
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the realms of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma,
the assembly of Bodhisattvas and immeasurable Śrāvakas, as well as all celestial immortals. May they arise as luminous terraces that extend beyond boundless realms and infinite Buddha-lands,
performing the work of Buddhas and universally perfuming all sentient beings, so that they may all resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
(Bowing down and reflecting, one thinks:

"I only pray that these incense and flowers may pervade all dust-motes and lands, making offerings to the Triple Gem of the ten directions. With celestial music, renowned incense, precious robes, and exquisite foods, may all boundless dust-motes and lands be fully adorned.

May my own body go to them all to cultivate offerings, continuing until the end of future kalpas; may these offerings of mine be uninterrupted. For the sake of seeking the Triple Gem, with great compassion to universally deliver sentient beings, may I attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
Having completed the offerings, with all due reverence (after one prostration, kneel and chant):
I bow my head to the Great Awakened Honored Ones of the ten directions, to all the Honored Dharmas and Bodhisattvas.
I take refuge in the Vajra Śarīra Stūpa and the Mahāratna-vistara-dhāraṇī. With single-minded devotion, I cultivate all wholesome dharmas through the merit of this divine mantra.
It possesses great majesty and power, capable of subduing all demonic armies and eradicating the grave sins of the Avīci hell.
It enables one’s present body and mind to personally behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and all Buddha-lands, and to recollect and know immeasurable past lives.
The Tathāgata’s consecration brings forth merit and wisdom beyond measure. Dragons and devas turn in reverent homage; spirits and ghosts look up with awe and veneration.

All petitions and aspirations shall ultimately be fulfilled. Universally benefiting sentient beings and extensively delivering all classes of living things, we therefore prostrate, receive and practice [these teachings] (one prostration, rising, and offering incense).
Seventh, to offer sincere homage and prostrate with single-minded devotion to the present Teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who sits upon the site of enlightenment: (Visualize thus:

"The nature of both the one who prostrates and the one to whom they prostrate is empty and tranquil; the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable. Within this site of my practice, like a jewel of Indra, the shadow of Śākyamuni Tathāgata appears; my own body and shadow likewise appear before the Tathāgata, meeting him face-to-face."
Sufficient. Homage and prostrations. (This is the three prostrations the presiding repentance master should perform.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One, King of Blazing Radiance Who Fulfills the Eastern Quarter and Eliminates Calamities while Extending Life.
(Verse same as before; however, change "Bhaiṣajyaguru Tathāgata" to "manifesting within," and apply this renaming to all subsequent instances).
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Amitāyus, the Teacher of the Western Quarter and the Guide who Leads Us Home.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Ratnasambhava of the Southern Quarter.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Subtle and Supreme of the North.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Great Exertion, Delightful to Behold by All Worlds.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Purely Established with Various Maṇi Jewels.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, the Light of the Body Manifesting All Colors.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, the Light of Samādhi. With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, the Radiance of Physical Marks and Features. With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, Supreme Wondrous Sound.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One, King of Immeasurable Sound;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One, King of Liberation; and to the World-Honored One, King of Beautiful Sound.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Purity, the World-Honored One who Bestows Pure Gifts.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, King of Majestic Power and Sovereignty. I prostrate with single-minded devotion to the World-Honored One Akṣobhya.
I prostrate with single-minded devotion to the World-Honored One Maitreya and the World-Honored One Śāriprabharāja.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as vast as empty space and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Honored Ones throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as vast as empty space and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all precious śarīras throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as vast as empty space and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom and the Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra-Rāja and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Māyā, the Mother of Great Compassion.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sthāvarā Pṛthivīdevatā and the Night Goddess Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vidyutprabhā;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, King of Secrets, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Subhūti.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhamati.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantadarśin and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Susamaya.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Paripūrṇagarbha.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the patriarchs of successive generations.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the great Śrāvakas of the ten directions and the three periods of time throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm.

I single-mindedly take refuge in and honor the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Sangha; the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, the World-Protecting Four Kings, the great celestial kings of the desire, form, and formless realms;
and all the virtuous deities who protect the stupas, temples, and monasteries of the Buddha’s relics and uphold the mantras.
Wang Hai Long bows his head in worship to the Eight Classes of Beings, the Celestial Bureaus, the Underworld, and all spirits of water, land, and air,
together with their retinues, as he offers the Eighth Universal Confession to the Triple Gem. (The assembly chants:)

With reverence, for the sake of the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the worlds of the ten directions who have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, I seek compassionate repentance (holding the incense burner and prostrating, visualize and say):

"Since beginningless time, I and all sentient beings have turned our backs on the Truth and followed after delusion, drowning in worldly toil and wandering through the six realms with no prospect of escape. Having failed to meet an enlightened teacher and failing to revere the Triple Gem, we have extensively committed manifold evils and feared not the three miserable realms."

Lacking faith in cause and effect and devoid of a sense of shame and remorse, one sinks into the three realms because of these reasons. Therefore, on this day, facing the Buddhas and before the stūpas of their relics, I give rise to great shame and remorse, extensively clarifying cause and effect, and engendering great dread.

I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem. I openly confess and repent my transgressions, severing all past evils and diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas. From this day forward, I shall seek the Way without regressing; for the sake of attaining Bodhi, I shall extensively benefit all sentient beings. The Buddhas of the ten directions possess great compassion.
"Listen to my confession; all shall attain purity. (Having visualized this, chant:
"The bhikṣu [Name] and others, together with all sentient beings, possess an inherently pure nature that is vast, penetrating, and perfectly luminous.

It encompasses all myriad virtues and is supremely wondrous and true. All Buddhas know it as one; all things share its same spiritual essence. Yet, we have all been conditioned by beginningless delusive thoughts."
They are driven by attachment and run headlong, like sand disturbing water. Shrouded in the turbidity of ignorance, they possess the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

They commit various evil karmas—the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten non-virtues—slandering the Mahāyāna, destroying the Triple Gem, defiling those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and encroaching upon the permanent property of the Sangha.

They cause schisms in the harmonious Sangha; they preach the Dharma impurely and instruct others according to what is not the Vinaya; they conceal their own transgressions; they indulge greed and anger through material support;

while internally coveting gain and offerings, they externally manifest dignified deportment; they break the precepts and disrupt the Dharma, acting in opposition to their teachers and elders, devoid of shame and remorse.
Evil thoughts burn fiercely. Such grave and minor offenses are beyond the power of words to fully describe.

By these causes and conditions, at the end of life one shall fall into the Avīci Hell, where one will endure all manner of sufferings amidst raging fires and mountains of blades for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, with no time of escape in sight.
Furthermore, today my body is entangled in manifold sufferings; illness and afflictions obstruct my spiritual practice. Now, before [the assembly]...
To the Śarīra Jewel Stūpa of our Original Teacher Śākyamuni (one prostration), together with all the Buddhas of the ten directions:
may you act as my compassionate fathers, taking pity on us and giving rise to great compassion. Accept my repentance, so that my heavy offenses may be extinguished and all evils eliminated;
may my body and mind be purified, and may I be fully satiated by the flavor of the Dharma. By reciting and upholding this secret dhāraṇī, may I realize and enter into all [realms].
The ocean of merit. May all vows be fulfilled and perfected (as stated in the invocation).
Having finished the repentance, take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem (one prostration).
The Ninth: Reverently Holding the Mantra Heart (The Leader says:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: "I now proclaim this King of Dharani Teachings.

This dharani can bring about the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi. If there are those who receive and uphold it, they will be able to eliminate all karmic offenses and their bodies shall attain..."

It is pure. Whether one seeks long life, seeks wealth and abundance, seeks official rank, seeks sons or daughters, or seeks rebirth in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—even for all such things sought, they shall all be accomplished.
Then he spoke the dhāraṇī, saying:
Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ (1) Oṃ (2) Vipulajvāle (3) Maṇiprabhe (4) Tathāta (5) Nirdaśane (6) Maṇi maṇi (7)
SVAḤ (8) | VIMALĀYE (9) | SARVA-GARBHE (10) | HŪṂ (11) | HŪṂ (12) | JVALA-BUDDHA-VIROCIṆI-GUHYA-ḌĀKINI-JVĀLE (16) | SVĀHĀ (17) ||
(Recite either one hundred and eight times or forty-nine times). After circumambulating the altar, the leader says:

"At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Established Secret Root Dhāraṇī, this great earth shook in six ways, and a great rain of jewels and great jewel-flowers fell everywhere."
The great assembly that had gathered was filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence,
for it enabled all wholesome dharmas to be fully accomplished and the realization of the ten stages (one prostration).
The Tenth Vow of Dedication (The assembly kneels and chants):
We bhikṣus [Name], etc., make this vow with a sincere heart. May we, by virtue of the compassion of all Buddhas, experience joy and serenity in body and mind.
I reverently rely upon the majestic power of the *dhāraṇī* to cause merit and wisdom to increase perfectly. I look up to the *śarīra*, its divine light illuminating my path to *bodhi*.
May I encounter the great vows of the Original Teacher and be gathered into the gate of Perfect Enlightenment. May my faculties become sharp and keen, and my right mindfulness become radiant.
May I practice the six *pāramitās* to perfection and attain liberation from all conditions. It is my hope that both self and others may enjoy these benefits wherever they go.
Manifesting the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants before one, he dwells at all times with his mind fully established in meditative contemplation.

Sweeping away the armies of Māra, he abides securely in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Proclaiming the wondrous meaning, he attains great wisdom while simultaneously practicing the great conduct.

Having personally received the transmission from Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, he fulfills the great vows while concurrently mobilizing great compassion. He succeeds to the legacy of Avalokiteśvara and Kṣitigarbha, extensively performing Buddha-works for the sake of all beings.
Benefiting sentient beings, they realize and enter the supernormal powers, fully ascending to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, I pray that all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions may together ascend to the field of peace and bliss, and collectively assemble in the abode of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). May all their aspirations and vows necessarily be fulfilled according to their hearts.
Should they hope for high office, long life, and increased rank and emolument, may their bodies become like adamant (*vajra*); and should they pray for wealth and prosperity...
My sons’ treasuries are overflowing, and my home abounds with jade trees. Upon the end of my life, I shall be reborn in the land of the Pure Land.

I further pray that the three miserable realms and evil paths may cease their suffering and still their bitterness. By means of the roots of goodness I have cultivated, may all beings be equally aided, so that they may all transcend saṃsāra and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Even if empty space were to come to an end, my vow would be boundless. I beseech the Buddha to grant his grace.
May the Compassionate One bear witness and grant his protection.
Having made this vow, take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem (one prostration).
(Stand up, settle the mind, adjust the robes, and add incense; the leader speaks, and the assembly responds in unison as follows):

Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions! Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions! Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions! (Holding the incense burner, bowing in greeting, and walking slowly around the altar.
Homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha!
Homage to the Medicine Master Buddha who Eliminates Calamities and Extends Life! Homage to Amitābha Buddha!
Homage to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Homage to the Honored Buddha Maitreya.
Homage to the Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī.
Homage to the Jewel Stūpa of the Relics.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Homage to Samantabhadra-rāja Bodhisattva.
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha-rāja Bodhisattva.
Homage to Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva. Homage to Avataṃsaka-mukha Bodhisattva.
(Having completed the circumambulation, return to your position and recite again:
Taking refuge in the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings shall perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, I vow that all sentient beings shall enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom becoming like the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings lead and govern great assemblies without any hindrance;
I pay homage to the noble assembly.

(Again, recite "Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. When exiting the altar and entering the meditation hall to observe, recite the mantra with single-minded focus. Once the incense has finished burning, proceed as you please.)
The Method for Repentance of Śāriputra (End)
